hints: Focus on the d-electron count left after the ion forms, since unpaired electrons in transition metals live in the 3d subshell.
Remember that 4s electrons are lost first, so write each atom as [Ar] 3d^x 4s^y then remove the 4s electrons before the 3d electrons.
Check if any of the resulting d^9, d^4 or d^2 configurations can be fully paired, and see what that tells you about all three ions.
walkthrough:
**Recall how transition metal ions form**

Think of it simply: when a transition metal becomes an ion, it loses its 4s electrons first, then its 3d electrons. This is the key rule for getting the electron count right.

General rule:
$$\text{atom } [\text{Ar}] \, 3d^x 4s^y \rightarrow \text{ion } [\text{Ar}] \, 3d^{x - \text{loss from d}}$$

**Work out Cu2+**

Copper is the tricky one. Its atom is $[\text{Ar}] \, 3d^{10} 4s^1$.

Remove two electrons (4s first, then one 3d):
$$\text{Cu}^{2+} = [\text{Ar}] \, 3d^9$$
A $d^9$ set must have one unpaired electron. So ion 1 qualifies.

**Work out Mn3+ and V3+**

Manganese atom is $[\text{Ar}] \, 3d^5 4s^2$. Remove three electrons (both 4s, then one 3d):
$$\text{Mn}^{3+} = [\text{Ar}] \, 3d^4$$
That gives four unpaired electrons.

Vanadium atom is $[\text{Ar}] \, 3d^3 4s^2$. Remove three electrons:
$$\text{V}^{3+} = [\text{Ar}] \, 3d^2$$
That gives two unpaired electrons. So ions 2 and 3 also qualify.

**Conclude the combination**

Since 1, 2 and 3 all contain one or more unpaired electrons, the combination with all three is correct.

options.A: Correct. Cu2+ is 3d9 with 1 unpaired, Mn3+ is 3d4 with 4 unpaired, and V3+ is 3d2 with 2 unpaired. All three contain unpaired electrons.
options.B: Incorrect. This option includes only 1 and 2. It wrongly leaves out V3+, which is 3d2 and clearly has two unpaired electrons.
options.C: Incorrect. This option includes only 2 and 3. It wrongly leaves out Cu2+, which is 3d9 and has one unpaired electron.
options.D: Incorrect. This option includes only 1. It wrongly excludes Mn3+ (3d4) and V3+ (3d2), both of which have multiple unpaired electrons.
